source.title: AdditiveLLM2: A Multi-modal Large Language Model for Additive Manufacturing

record.file_problem: None noted; the supplied text contains the full paper. Its title differs from the title in the metadata.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream benchmark performance across models with different parameter counts, but does not reproduce a held-out-loss scaling-law experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper mentions scaling laws in background and cites Kaplan et al., but reports no held-out pretraining-loss fits, extrapolations, or compute-optimal allocation results. The benchmark comparisons across differently sized model families bear narrowly on V6. Domain-adaptation stage results are not rows for scaling-law versions.
record.test_reason: This is a domain-adaptation study. Its only size-related evidence compares three base models from different families and generations (Qwen3-VL 8B, Gemma 3 12B, Gemma 4 31B). Pretraining data, architecture and post-training all differ, so size is confounded and no scale trend or loss relation can be read. Scaling laws and Kaplan et al. appear only in background, plus an informal attribution of Qwen's weaker results to fewer parameters. No loss, fits, extrapolation, allocation or controlled downstream scaling is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, with one addition. The authors conclude that DAPT plus visual instruction tuning on about 45M text tokens (3 epochs per stage) lets models outperform their base counterparts on AM benchmarks. The VIT Gemma-3-12B variant is best on vision tasks and exceeds 90% on general knowledge. The larger Gemma-4-31B shows greater general-knowledge ability but similar visual-task performance. They also note image DAPT tends to degrade performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates domain adaptation on additive-manufacturing benchmarks rather than fitting or testing the original scaling-law method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported benchmark outcomes vary by model and task; image-based performance is not consistently better for the larger model.

fits_no_version.finding: Across three confounded base models, the largest (Gemma 4 31B) scores far higher on AM general-knowledge short answer (>75 vs ~15) but similar or worse on AM image tasks. The authors informally attribute Qwen3-8B's weaker AM results to its fewer parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Across model families, larger open-weight models show better domain-knowledge recall but no consistent advantage on domain vision tasks; this is uncontrolled and not a scaling-law test.

record.problems: The size comparisons are across different model families and are not a controlled scaling study. The reported comparisons do not establish a general or predictable relation between model size and downstream performance.
record.rows_left_out: No scaling-law or held-out-loss results were reported. Domain-adaptation stage comparisons and other benchmark outcomes were omitted because they do not test the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation.
No shape variation at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fits in other modalities or in fine-tuning or transfer; the domain-adaptation token count is not varied.
No controlled size sweep within one family and no link between downstream scores and pretraining loss; the three models differ in family and generation.
No exponents or splits are fitted.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'tests' relation overstates the evidence. R1 and R3 were misread: they compare Gemma 4 training stages, not sizes. No verdicts are given because no version is actually tested.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured against parameter count, token count, or compute.
No small-run power-law fit or larger-run loss prediction is reported.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token allocation law is tested.
The study does not vary architecture details at fixed parameter count to measure loss.
The study does not test power-law scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
The model-size comparisons involve different model families and do not test a controlled scaling trend or relate downstream performance to pretraining loss.
No scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits are fitted or compared across setups.
